provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Numbers and indices
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the laws of indices.
The students should be able to express numbers in standard form.
Introduction:
We have learned about whole numbers and fractions. Today we will learn how to work with exponents and write very large or small numbers easily.
Content:
Laws of indices tell us how to handle expressions with powers. For example, when multiplying same bases, we add the exponents: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷. Standard form is a way to write numbers as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10. For example, the population of Nigeria is about 2.06 × 10⁸ people. We use standard form in science and when dealing with very large amounts like the national budget in naira.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to convert given numbers like the price of a danfo bus or the cost of a kerosene stove into standard form.
Evaluation questions:
What is the value of 3² × 3³?
Express 2500000 in standard form.
Explain why we use standard form in mathematics.
Summary:
Today we learned the laws of indices and how to write numbers in standard form, which helps us work with very large or small numbers easily.

topics.title: Logarithms
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to use log tables to find values.
The students should be able to solve multiplication problems using logarithms.
Introduction:
We have learned about exponents. Logarithms are the opposite of exponents and help us solve certain types of problems.
Content:
A logarithm tells us what exponent we need for a given base. For example, log₁₀ 100 = 2 because 10² = 100. We use log tables to find logarithm values when we don't have calculators. To multiply numbers using logs, we add their logs and then find the antilog. For example, to multiply 45 by 82, we find log 45 + log 82 = 1.6532 + 1.9138 = 3.567, then antilog 3.567 ≈ 3690. This method was very useful before calculators, especially for traders calculating market profits.
Class activity:
Students will use log tables to solve multiplication problems involving prices of goods in the market.
Evaluation questions:
What is log₁₀ 1000?
Show how to use logs to multiply 25 by 40.
Why might someone use logarithms instead of direct multiplication?
Summary:
Logarithms help us find exponents and can make multiplication easier by turning it into addition.

topics.title: Variation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve direct variation problems.
The students should be able to solve inverse variation problems.
Introduction:
We have learned about different types of relationships between numbers. Today we will study how quantities can vary directly or inversely.
Content:
Direct variation means when one quantity increases, the other also increases at a constant rate. For example, the more bags of rice you buy, the higher the total cost. If y varies directly as x, we write y = kx where k is the constant. Inverse variation means when one quantity increases, the other decreases. For example, the more people sharing a large pot of soup, the smaller each portion becomes. If y varies inversely as x, we write y = k/x. Joint variation combines both types, like when the cost of producing plantain chips depends on both the amount of plantains and the price of oil.
Class activity:
Students will solve problems about sharing money among friends (direct) and dividing land among families (inverse).
Evaluation questions:
If 5 workers can build a house in 20 days, how long would 10 workers take?
The price of a phone is inversely proportional to the number of people buying it. If 4 people buy, each pays N2000. How much would one person pay?
Give an example of direct variation from everyday life.
Summary:
Direct and inverse variation help us understand how different quantities relate to each other in real life situations.

topics.title: Probability
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to calculate probability of simple events.
The students should be able to find experimental probability.
Introduction:
We have learned about fractions and ratios. Probability uses these ideas to measure how likely something is to happen.
Content:
Probability is the measure of how likely an event is to happen, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). For simple events, we calculate probability as number of favorable outcomes divided by total possible outcomes. For example, the probability of picking a red ball from a bag with 3 red and 2 blue balls is 3/5. Experimental probability comes from actually doing experiments and recording results. For example, if we flip a coin 20 times and get heads 12 times, the experimental probability of heads is 12/20 = 3/5. We use probability in weather forecasts, like predicting if it will rain during harmattan season.
Class activity:
Students will flip coins or spin spinners 50 times each and record their results to find experimental probability.
Evaluation questions:
What is the probability of rolling a 3 on a normal die?
A market seller sold 50 oranges, 30 were good and 20 were bad. What is the probability of picking a good orange?
How is experimental probability different from theoretical probability?
Summary:
Probability helps us understand and predict chances of events happening in our daily lives.

topics.title: Circle geometry
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify properties of chords and angles in circles.
The students should be able to apply circle theorems to solve problems.
Introduction:
We have learned about basic shapes. Today we will study special properties of circles and the angles within them.
Content:
In circle geometry, we study special properties. A chord is a straight line connecting two points on the circle. The angle at the center is twice the angle at the circumference when both angles stand on the same arc. For example, if angle at center is 100°, then angle at circumference is 50°. Angles in the same segment are equal. If two chords intersect inside a circle, the products of their segments are equal. These theorems help us solve problems about round objects like wheels, traditional round drums, and circular market stalls.
Class activity:
Students will draw circles with chords and measure angles to verify circle theorems.
Evaluation questions:
State the theorem relating the angle at the center to the angle at the circumference.
In a circle, angle AOB is 80°. What is angle ACB if both angles stand on the same arc?
How can circle theorems help us solve real-world problems?
Summary:
Circle theorems give us special rules about angles and chords that help us solve geometry problems involving circles.

topics.title: Constructions
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to construct bisectors and angles using compass and ruler.
The students should be able to construct different types of triangles.
Introduction:
We have learned about different shapes. Today we will learn how to draw exact geometric shapes using only a compass and ruler.
Content:
Geometric construction is drawing shapes using only compass and ruler without measuring. To construct an angle bisector, we draw an arc from the vertex, then from those points draw more arcs that intersect. The line from vertex to intersection is the bisector. To construct a triangle, we need to know either three sides, two sides and included angle, or two angles and one side. For example, to construct a triangle with sides 6cm, 7cm, and 8cm, we draw one side, then use compass to mark the other sides. These skills are useful for designing local patterns, building traditional structures, and creating art.
Class activity:
Students will construct triangles with given side lengths and angle bisectors on paper using compass and ruler.
Evaluation questions:
What tools do we need for geometric construction?
Describe how to construct a 60° angle using only compass and ruler.
Why might someone need to construct triangles instead of just drawing them?
Summary:
Geometric construction teaches us to create exact shapes using only compass and ruler, developing important spatial reasoning skills.

topics.title: Graphs of quadratic functions
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to plot the parabola of a quadratic function.
The students should be able to read the roots from a quadratic graph.
Introduction:
We have learned about linear graphs that make straight lines. Today we will study quadratic graphs that make curves called parabolas.
Content:
A quadratic function is in the form y = ax² + bx + c where a, b, c are numbers and a ≠ 0. When we plot these points, we get a U-shaped curve called a parabola. The highest or lowest point is called the vertex. The roots are where the graph crosses the x-axis. For example, for y = x² - 4, the roots are at x = 2 and x = -2. We can find these by setting y = 0 and solving. Quadratic graphs model many real situations like the height of a ball thrown in the air or the profit of a small business over time.
Class activity:
Students will plot the quadratic function y = x² - 3x + 2 and identify its roots and vertex.
Evaluation questions:
What shape is made by a quadratic function?
How do you find the roots from a quadratic graph?
Give an example of a real situation that could be modeled by a quadratic graph.
Summary:
Quadratic graphs are parabolas that help us visualize and solve equations with squared terms.

topics.title: Statistics: pie charts
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to calculate angles for pie chart segments.
The students should be able to draw and interpret pie charts.
Introduction:
We have learned about bar graphs and line graphs. Today we will study pie charts, which show parts of a whole.
Content:
A pie chart is a circular graph divided into segments to show how a whole is divided. To draw a pie chart, we first find the angle for each segment using: angle = (value/total) × 360°. For example, if a market has 40% yam sellers, 30% rice sellers, and 30% bean sellers, the angles would be 144°, 108°, and 108°. We use protractors to draw these angles from the center. Pie charts are useful for showing how government money is spent, how students spend their time, or the ethnic composition of a community.
Class activity:
Students will create a pie chart showing how they spend their 24-hour day in categories like sleep, school, meals, and leisure.
Evaluation questions:
How do you calculate the angle for a segment in a pie chart?
In a class of 40 students, 25 play football, 10 play basketball, and 5 play no sport. Draw the pie chart.
Why might someone prefer a pie chart over a bar graph for certain data?
Summary:
Pie charts help us visualize how parts make up a whole using angles in a circle.

topics.title: Everyday arithmetic
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to calculate tax, interest, and sharing problems.
The students should be able to solve BECE style arithmetic problems.
Introduction:
We have learned about percentages and fractions. Today we will apply these to real-life situations like taxes, interest, and sharing money.
Content:
Tax is a percentage of income or goods that goes to the government. For example, if VAT is 7.5%, a N1000 item will have N75 added as tax. Interest is money paid for borrowing or saving. Simple interest is calculated as I = PRT/100 where P is principal, R is rate, T is time. For example, N10000 at 5% per year for 2 years gives N1000 interest. Sharing problems divide amounts in given ratios. For example, if N30000 is shared between A, B, C in ratio 3:2:1, A gets N15000, B gets N10000, and C gets N5000. These skills help with managing family budgets, calculating profits in market trading, and understanding bank statements.
Class activity:
Students will solve problems about calculating VAT on goods, finding interest on savings, and sharing money among family members.
Evaluation questions:
If VAT is 7.5%, how much VAT is paid on a phone costing N45000?
Find the simple interest on N20000 at 6% per year for 3 years.
N60000 is shared between three people in ratio 3:2:1. How much does each person get?
Summary:
Everyday arithmetic helps us manage money wisely by understanding taxes, interest, and sharing.

topics.title: Revision and BECE practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve past BECE questions.
The students should be able to identify common mistakes and correct them.
Introduction:
We have learned many topics this term. Today we will practice exam questions to prepare for our BECE examination.
Content:
Revision means going over what we have learned to strengthen our understanding. For BECE practice, we solve past examination questions to understand the question patterns and time management. Common mistakes include not reading questions carefully, mixing up formulas, and poor time allocation. When marking, we look for correct methods, not just answers. For example, in a problem about sharing money, showing the ratio setup is important even if the final calculation has an error. Practicing with BECE questions helps us understand what examiners expect and how to present our solutions clearly.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past BECE mathematics questions and then present their solutions to the class.
Evaluation questions:
Solve this BECE style problem: If 5 books cost N7500, how much will 8 books cost?
Find the area of a rectangle 12cm by 8cm.
What are three common mistakes students make in mathematics exams?
Summary:
Regular practice with past questions helps us prepare better for examinations by familiarizing us with question types and improving our problem-solving skills.
